W H A T ' S  T H E  P R O M P T  C A C H E ?
It's short-term memory Claude keeps during your chat, so it doesn't have to reread your entire conversation every time
you send a message. After an hour, the prompt cache goes cold. Then the next message makes Claude reread your
entire conversation at the normal cost, which can really eat into your limits. Seeing that at a glance saves you tokens in
the long run.

Want to go deeper? My full video on Claude mods: youtube.com/watch?v=lDrAZ1wAyVs
A slim bar above your chat box that shows what's left of your usage for the week.

# Julian's Voice

Julian writes like a teammate typing between tasks: short, plain, first person, specific. Most messages are 1-3 sentences of 10-35 words. He goes long only to explain a cause or announce a change, and then he writes paragraphs, not lists.

## This skill overrides chat-style rules

Caveman mode, terse-output rules, and the "no hedging" rule in CLAUDE.md govern how Claude talks to Julian. They do not apply to drafts written as Julian. His real voice uses full sentences, articles, and softeners like "I think" and "Not sure if ...?". Keep them. If a humanizer pass runs afterwards, this skill wins on conflicts.

## Before drafting

Read the examples file for the context you are writing in. Match its length and shape before you match its words.

| Context | Examples file |
|---|---|
| Chat DM or channel | `examples/chat.md` |
| PR review comment or reply | `examples/pr-comments.md` |
| PR title, PR description, commit message | `examples/pr-and-commits.md` |
| GitHub issue or issue comment | `examples/issues.md` |

## After drafting

Once a draft is final and meant to be posted, log it so Julian's later edits can improve this skill. Pass the draft text on stdin:

```bash
uv run ~/.claude/skills/julian-voice/scripts/feedback.py draft --context <context> --target <target>
```

| Context | `--context` | `--target` |
|---|---|---|
| Chat | `chat` | server and channel, or DM partner |
| PR review comment | `pr-comment` | PR URL |
| PR description / title | `pr-description` / `pr-title` | PR URL |
| Commit message | `commit` | absolute path of the local repo |
| Issue comment / new issue | `issue-comment` / `issue` | issue URL, or repo URL for a new issue |

Log one entry per piece of text. A PR title and its description are two entries. When Julian asks to review voice feedback, follow `FEEDBACK.md` in this skill's directory.

## Shape by context

**Chat.** Median 19 words. Lowercase starts and no final period are normal. Casual words are normal: "y'all", "gonna", "cuz", "rq", "iirc", "lol". End with a `:shortcode:` emoji when one fits (`:+1:`, `:joy:`, `:shrug:`, `:facepalm:`). Greet only when opening a conversation or channel post: "Howdy", "Morning y'all,", "Hey team,". Links go on their own line with a one-line description. Times look like "1230 EST".

**PR review comment.** Median 16 words. Pick one of three forms:
- A bare fragment for trivial fixes: "lingering import", "Can be removed", "Use `pytest.approx` instead."
- A lowercase label: `nitpick:`, `suggestion:`, `question:`, followed by a direct sentence and its reason.
- A question for judgment calls: "Would it make sense to ...?", "Is there a way to ...?", "What do you think about ...?", followed by "Mostly asking since ...".

Put code after "something like this:" in an untagged fence. Identifiers go in backticks. Link docs as evidence.

**Replying to review.**
- Accepting: "Good catch, changed." / "Good point." / "Thanks for catching that." plus what you did.
- Your own mistake: "Whoops," / "Shoot," / "my bad" plus the fix in one clause.
- Changing your mind later: "Coming back to this, ..." or "The more I thought about it, ...".
- Pushing back: concede part first ("I agree, but ...", "True, and ..."), then the concrete reason. For a strong position use "I'm going to push against ... because ...".
- Approving: "LGTM, rebase your branch and then I'll approve :thumbsup:".

**PR title.** Check the repo's recent history with `git log` first. If the repo already follows its own format, such as `type(scope): subject` or a leading `(#123)` issue number, use that format. Otherwise the format is `type: subject`.
- **Types:** `feat`, `fix`, `ci`, `chore`, `doc`, `revert`, `test`. A breaking change is `feat!:`.
- **Subject:** a lowercase imperative clause with no trailing period: "feat: give the connector egress to its origins".
- **Joining items:** use ", " ("fix: cap workers at 50 jobs, raise root volume to 50GB, fix the Docker cleanup").
- **Why the title matters:** when the repo squash-merges, the title becomes the commit on the default branch.

The older styles (`KEY-N - Adding ...`, `NOREF - ...`) in `examples/pr-and-commits.md` are history. Use them only when Julian asks for that style.

**PR description.** Median 20 words. Open with the non-obvious fact, the reason, a link ("See <url>"), or "Also ...". The title already says what the PR does, so the description starts where the title stops. For several changes, use `- ` bullets starting with Added/Updated/Removed/Moved/Renamed, or "`identifier` updated from `X` to `Y`". Give each reason inline ("as", "since", "in favor of") or in a nested sub-bullet. Show proof with a short lead line: "Confirmed working here: <workflow run url>", a fenced error, or a captioned screenshot. End after the last fact. Headers appear only in long descriptions, and they name an area ("## Helm Related Changes").

**Commit message.** The subject follows the same format rule as the PR title: the repo's own format when it has one, otherwise `type: subject`. In someone else's repo, copy the owner's convention for the body too, judged from their recent commits in `git log`:
- **Owner writes subject-only commits:** write a subject only, such as `fix(quests): Dragon's Breath farming hint and Trinity Gem boss capture`.
- **Owner writes bodies:** wrap at 80 columns and walk the cause. Open with what is broken ("Without this patch applied, ..."), trace it through exact `Class#method` names, then say what "This patch ..." changes and what stays unaffected. `examples/pr-and-commits.md` has a full example.
- **Repo has no convention:** write one to three short sentences saying why, in his voice.

```
fix: publish releases with an image that has the gh cli

The release job was using an image without gh, so it failed before publishing.
```

**GitHub issue.** Start with "As an engineer, I want to ..." or a plain problem statement. Follow with evidence (error text, workflow run link). Then bold labels on their own lines: `**TASKS:**`, `**AC:**`, `**QA:**`, plus `**REPOS:**` or `**References:**` when useful. Tasks name exact variables, paths, and values. AC are observable outcomes. Small issues can be one or two lines.

**Issue comment.** Open with @mentions when addressing people, with the question on the same line or the next. Status updates are past tense and carry proof: "Deployed to dev: <url>", "Confirmed working in dev after rerunning the previously failed run." Close issues with "Marking as won't do, as ..." or "Implemented with <link>". Put any "cc @Name" line last. No "!" and no emoji.

## Habits across contexts

- **Requests:** "When you get a chance, do you mind ...?" plus why. "Please" is rare.
- **Hedges:** one per message, placed before the claim, followed by the reason. Use "I think", "Not sure if ...?", "I believe", "probably", "imo", or "(could be wrong on this)".
- **Questions:** state your own guess and end with "right?" or "correct?". Ask what someone meant before assuming: "Not sure I follow what you mean by that?"
- **Causes:** "The issue is that ...". Walk the chain step by step, use exact identifiers, and paste the error line.
- **Linkers:** "That way ...", "On top of that, ...", "instead of", "for some reason", "e.g.", "~" for approximate numbers ("~3-5 minutes").
- **Emphasis:** `_underscore_` italics or one word in CAPS ("MUCH", "NOT"). Bold appears only as issue section labels.
- **Humor:** dry, aimed at himself or at the tools, never at the reviewer.

## Swap these for his forms

| Instead of | He writes |
|---|---|
| Em dash, en dash, or semicolon | A comma, a period, or a new sentence |
| "Additionally" / "Furthermore" | "Also" / "On top of that," |
| "i.e." | "e.g." or "for example" |
| "Great question!" / "Thanks for the thorough review!" | Get straight to the answer |
| "Hope this helps" / "Let me know your thoughts!" | Stop after the last fact. Use "Let me know" only when tied to a specific action. |
| `## Summary` / `## Changes` / `**Label:** value` in a PR | Plain bullets or 1-3 sentences |
| Turning a conversational message into a bullet list | Prose. Lists only for truly parallel items. |
| Placeholder sample data (`device-1`) | Realistic values (UUIDs, real timestamps) |
| Literal emoji glyphs | `:shortcode:` |
| "You're absolutely right" | "You are correct," / "Yep you're right." |
| Restating the PR title as the first line | The non-obvious fact, reason, or link |

## Quick prompt

Short, plain, first person. One to three sentences unless explaining a cause. Use the format of the context: lowercase labels in reviews, past-tense proof in issues, -ing titles, commits in the repo owner's format. Soften with "I think" or "Not sure if ...?" and give the reason. Back claims with a link. No em dashes, semicolons, headers in comments, bold outside issue labels, sign-offs, or recaps. Read the matching examples file first.
